1. Loop bands: These are the most common types of resistance bands and are often used for leg exercises such as squats, leg presses, and lateral band walks. They are typically made of latex or rubber and come in different resistance levels from light to heavy.

1. Bicep curls: Stand on the center of the resistance band while holding the handles with palms up. Keep your elbows tight to the sides of your body and curl the handles up toward your shoulders.

2. Squats: Place the resistance band around both legs, just above your knees, and stand with your feet hip-width apart. Push your hips back and lower your body into a squat position while keeping the resistance band taut.

3. Lateral band walks: Place the resistance band around both legs, just above your ankles, and stand with feet hip-width apart. Take small steps to the side while keeping the band taut and maintain a squat position.

content:Speaker assistant says: The history of pet grooming techniques and equipment dates back to many centuries, with the early forms of grooming focused on the utilitarian purpose of pets; for work, protection, or pest control. Over time, however, pet grooming has evolved into an art form, with varied styles of grooming techniques being applied to different companion animal species. The following is a comprehensive account of the evolution of pet grooming techniques and equipment, including the different methods and styles of grooming applied to various companion animal species throughout history.

Ancient Rome and Egypt
Pet grooming has been around since ancient times, with evidence of pet grooming dating back to ancient Egypt, where dogs were groomed with combs, brushes, and shears. Egyptians were known to shave their cats to worship their cat goddess known as Bastet. In ancient Rome, dogs were also groomed with different instruments for various purposes. For example, hunting dogs were groomed to have a short, sleek coat to minimize drag and to prevent brush and twigs from getting caught in their fur.

Middle Ages
During the Middle Ages, pet grooming techniques became more refined and established as a profession. Dog groomers were often employed by noble families to keep their pets clean and well-cared for. Groomers during this era relied on hand tools such as combs, brushes, and scissors for grooming. 

Renaissance
The Renaissance period marked significant progress in pet grooming techniques, with dog grooming becoming more sophisticated. Aristocrats of the time often had their dogs groomed to look imposing and elegant. As dog shows became popular, the grooming of dogs became a subject of art, and dog breeders began to develop specific grooming styles for particular breeds.

Victorian Era
During the Victorian era, pets became increasingly popular as status symbols, and pet grooming became more professionalized. Professional pet groomers began to emerge, and new tools such as clippers, trimmers, and dryers were invented. 

Twentieth Century
The 20th century marked a transformative turning point in the evolution of pet grooming. The introduction of steel blades to clippers and the electric-powered clipper revolutionized grooming. Electric dryers also improved the speed and efficiency of pet grooming. Professional groomers became increasingly skilled and could now create elaborate grooming styles such as poodles in stereotypical clip shapes.

"This small city of Greeley, in which I am staying, is so beautiful that one may easily imagine that he is in paradise. As one observes, the owners of these houses spend their leisure time in toil, watering their private yards and trimming their gardens. This is all they appear to do ..."
"I stayed there six months and never did I see a person or a family actually enjoying themselves, even on summer nights when breezes waft over the city as if in a dream. The dance began after an evening service, and was led by the church's pastor, who, according to Qutb's breathless account, lowered the lights and put a recording of "Baby, It's Cold Outside" on the turntable in an effort to get the few remaining wallflowers out on the dance floor. "The dance hall convulsed to the tunes on the gramophone and was full of bounding feet and seductive legs," Qutb later wrote. "Arms circled waists, lips met lips, chests met chests, and the atmosphere was full of passion."

It may be, of course, that Qutb's Islamism, metastasized into bin Laden's Islamism, is indeed shocked beyond measure at the thought of women's equality, gay dignity and the more lurid aspects of American popular culture. But the shock goes far deeper than anything that has happened in America since the 1960s. content:Speaker user says: Given the text: TED offers scientists and other experts a platform to provide scientific information directly to millions of people around the world. It’s a responsibility we take seriously. First and foremost, that information has to be scientifically credible.
Science isn’t a set of truths written in stone. It’s an approach to discovering truths about the world.
Explanatory theories are tested against observational evidence. If the evidence offers support for a theory, it may become accepted as part of current scientific consensus.
New hypotheses, new forms of experiments, new tools, and new ways of gathering data are constantly adding to what scientists can discover. Which means that scientific ideas are always subject to change.
At TED, we strive to present science in a way that is both compelling and 100% credible. Scientific claims by our speakers should be based on data that has survived scrutiny by experts in the field. Speakers should be transparent about the basis for any factual claims, and the scientific evidence for them.
Usually, such ideas first find expression via publication in a peer-reviewed journal and come from individuals and teams with the qualifications to generate and assess such ideas. If a claim is based on unpublished work, that fact must be made clear in the talk.
TED employs a science curator as well as fact-checkers and topic-specific advisors. Before a speaker is invited to the TED stage, we strive to ensure that their work has been peer-reviewed, and that they are well regarded by other scientists. And we rely on you, TED’s audience, to alert us to questions or concerns, whether about a TEDx talk, a post on ideas.ted.com, or an outdated talk from the mainstage.
Is it OK to simplify?
In a short talk, it’s impossible to include all the nuance of scientific research. TED’s goal is to make science accessible to a wide audience. This inevitably means that some scientific concepts have to be simplified. But it’s important that they not be simplified to the point of becoming misleading. We encourage speakers to add footnotes to their talks if need be.
Scientific journals and some scientific conferences discourage scientists from saying anything other than the direct findings of their work. At TED, we’re interested in understanding the potential implications of new scientific findings. This is essential in motivating further exploration and discovery.
So we are comfortable inviting scientists to speculate on the potential implications and applications of their work. But it’s also important that they distinguish clearly between what has already been achieved and what might be to come.
We strive to admit when we make a mistake and make every effort to correct it, up to and including removing content.
Much like science, TED attempts to advance ideas worth spreading via dialogue and debate, new data and new hypotheses. And much like science, TED’s science content and these standards will be constantly up for review and revision. In the meantime, we will continue to strive to bring you ideas that explore the wonder, ingenuity, passion, skepticism, and facts of science.
For the love of facts!
Watch a collection of wonderful, fact-loving talks that’ll encourage you to not just face the facts, but embrace them.

content:Speaker user says: Given that skiing and snowboarding’s most basic goal is to avoid falling, balance is obviously important. The off-season can be a good time to work on balance skills either at the gym or at home.
Related to balance, proprioception is the technical term for the sense of knowing where your body parts are in space and relative to each other. When performing the complex movements involved in skiing or snowboarding, good balance and proprioception are key.
For skiers, the SkiA Ski Trainer ($70) directly addresses these abilities. The product also gives skiers an excuse to actually put on their ski boots in the middle of the summer. The SkiA Trainer has straps that hold different-sized blocks on the ski-boot soles. The smaller blocks are more challenging. The basic idea is to simulate skiing movements while balancing on the blocks.
While not ski-specific, slacklines are also popular and effective for off-season balance training. Lindsey Vonn, for one, loves to test herself on the slightly springy webbing that measures an inch-or-two wide.
Eirik Hole, the strength and conditioning coach for the women’s U.S. Ski Team, incorporates balance work as part of his regimen for the world-class ski racers. He says recreational skiers and snowboarders can begin with simple exercises that do not require any equipment.
Certified personal trainer Lynette Talbott teaches a ski-conditioning class each fall at the Tahoe Center for Health and Sports Performance in Truckee, California. For balance, she starts students with simple single-leg balancing and then single-leg balancing on an unstable surface. For a cost-free option at home, a sofa cushion can serve as an unstable surface.
According to Talbott, simultaneous strength and balance training is falling out of favor in light of exercise research studies. An example would be doing overhead dumbbell presses while standing on a BOSU ball (those half-balls found at most gyms). While both are good activities, they don’t need to be done at the same time.
In fact, Hole uses BOSU balls with his U.S. Ski Team athletes for balance-specific exercises. The skiers jump forward and from each side on and off the balls. He also has them use balance boards and trampolines during dry-land training.
A little balance training can be a productive way to spend a little time in the summer. The weather may be warm now, but a little effort could pay off when the snow falls.

content:Speaker assistant says: Sure, here are some exercises that you can do at home to improve your balance and proprioception for skiing:

1. Single-leg stance: Stand on one leg and try to maintain your balance without wobbling or touching the ground. Start with 30 seconds on each leg and work your way up to 60 seconds.

2. Single-leg stance with eyes closed: stand on one leg and close your eyes. Try to maintain your balance without peeking. This is more challenging and will help to improve your proprioception.

3. Pistol squats: Place one foot on a sturdy chair, bench or step while the other leg is extended in front of you. Slowly lower yourself into a squat with the elevated leg, then stand back up. Repeat for 10-15 reps on each side.

4. Wobble board exercise: Stand on a wobble board or balance disc and try to maintain your balance. Increase the difficulty by closing your eyes or performing rotational movements while standing on the discs.

5. Side leg raises: Lie down on your side with your legs straight. Lift your top leg up, keeping it straight, then lower it down. Repeat for 10-15 reps on each side.

Remember to start with easier exercises and gradually work your way up to more challenging movements. Also, mix up your routine to keep things interesting and challenging. context:FoxNOV Bike Phone Mount keywords: balance, proprioception, skiing, exercises tags: Bear KompleX, Gymnastics Grips, Camera Grip, Canon EOS 40D, Focusing Screen

content:Speaker assistant says: Preparing for a snowboarding trip can be an exciting and thrilling experience. However, it can also be overwhelming if you’re unsure about what to expect. To ensure that you have the best time possible, we’ve compiled a comprehensive guide to help you prepare effectively. Here’s everything you need to know, step-by-step.

1. Determine the Destination
The first step in preparing for a snowboarding trip is to decide where you want to go. There are numerous snowboarding destinations around the world, including New Zealand, Japan, Canada, Europe, and the United States. Each location has its own unique features, including terrain, climate, and culture, so it’s essential to choose the one that suits your preferences.

2. Research and Book Accommodations
Once you’ve decided on your destination, the next step is to research and book your accommodations. Depending on your budget, you may choose to stay in a hotel, hostel, or rental home. Be sure to check the proximity of your accommodation to the slopes, as this can significantly impact your trip’s overall experience.

3. Gather Necessary Equipment
Before you begin snowboarding, you’ll need to ensure you have the necessary equipment. At a minimum, you’ll require a snowboard, bindings, boots, goggles, and a helmet. Depending on your experience level and the conditions, you may also want to consider purchasing additional equipment, such as gloves, a jacket, or extra padding.

4. Wear Appropriate Attire
When snowboarding, it’s crucial to wear appropriate attire to stay comfortable and safe. Consider packing thermal and waterproof clothing, layers, gloves, a beanie, a face mask, a backpack, and other gear to meet your needs.

5. Get in Shape
Snowboarding requires a significant amount of physical exertion, so it’s essential to prepare your body beforehand. Cardiovascular exercise, weight training, stretching, or yoga are excellent ways to increase your stamina and reduce the chances of injury.

6. Make Travel Arrangements
Once you know where you’re going, book your travel arrangements. Whether you choose to drive or fly, be sure to plan your journey carefully and make arrangements for any necessary transfers, rental cars or accommodations, and transportation to the resort.

7. Book Activities and Lessons
If you’re new to snowboarding, it’s recommended to take a course or two to learn the basics before hitting the slopes. Even experienced riders may benefit from an advanced lesson to hone their skills. Additionally, research the local area for other winter activities to enjoy, such as ice skating, sledding, or hot springs.

8. Prepare for Health Emergencies
Finally, it’s essential to plan for any health emergencies that may arise. Be sure to pack a first-aid kit and any necessary medication, and review your travel insurance policy to ensure you’re covered for any accidents that may occur.

Planning a snowboarding trip can be an exhilarating and unforgettable experience. By following these outlined steps, you can prepare effectively, stay safe, and make the most of your trip. content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! Choosing the right snowboard size and shape is essential to ensure that you have a positive experience when snowboarding. Here are some tips to help you choose the right snowboard size and shape for your level of experience:

1. Determine Your Riding Style
The first step in selecting the right snowboard is to determine your riding style. Are you more interested in riding park, groomers, or backcountry terrain? Different types of snowboards will work better for different styles. 2. Consider Your Experience Level
Next, consider your experience level. If you’re a beginner, you’ll typically want to choose a shorter, more flexible board that is easy to control. Intermediate and advanced riders may prefer longer, stiffer boards that offer more stability and control at high speeds. 3. Know Your Height and Weight
Your height and weight are also crucial factors to consider when selecting a snowboard. A general rule of thumb is that the board should come up to somewhere between your chin and nose when held up vertically. Additionally, heavier riders may prefer a wider board to ensure that there is enough surface area for adequate control. 4. Choose the Right Shape
The shape of the snowboard also makes a significant difference in how it performs. There are three primary shapes, including camber, rocker, and hybrid. Camber boards are best for riders who want a more responsive, stable ride, while rocker boards are more forgiving and easy to maneuver. Hybrid boards are a combination of both. 5. Consider the Terrain
Finally, consider the terrain you’ll be riding on. If you plan to ride mostly groomed runs, you may prefer a narrower board with a longer tail. For backcountry or powder riding, a wider, shorter board is typically better as it provides more float and control. Choosing the right snowboard size and shape can be challenging, but by considering the factors listed above, you’ll be well on your way to selecting a board that will meet your needs and level of experience. context:Snowboarding requires careful selection of equipment to ensure a safe and enjoyable experience on the mountain. content:Speaker assistant says: When it comes to snowboarding gear, there are several factors to consider to ensure that you have the best experience on the mountain. Here are some comprehensive tips to help you select the best snowboarding gear based on your personal preferences, terrain types, weather conditions, or specific activities such as freestyle or backcountry riding:

1. Snowboard: The snowboard is the most important piece of equipment for a snowboarder. The size and shape of the snowboard will depend on your personal preferences, style of riding, and the terrain you will be riding on. If you are a beginner, go for a soft flex snowboard with a flat or rocker profile. For freestyle riding, look for a shorter, twin-tip board with a medium flex. For big mountain riding or backcountry, a longer, directional board with a stiffer flex and a camber profile would be ideal.

2. Bindings: Snowboard bindings connect your boots to your snowboard and play a crucial role in transferring your movements to the board. Look for bindings with a high back for extra support, and adjustable straps for a customized fit. Also, consider the type of riding you will be doing - soft flex bindings are ideal for park, while stiff flex bindings are best for backcountry.

3. Boots: Snowboarding boots provide support and comfort to your feet while riding. Choose boots that fit well, are comfortable, and provide sufficient support. The flex rating of boots typically ranges from 1 to 10, with 1 being the softest and 10 being the stiffest. Soft flex boots are ideal for beginners, while stiffer boots are suitable for advanced riders.

4. Jacket and Pants: Snowboarding jackets and pants are crucial in keeping you warm, dry, and comfortable on the mountain. Look for jackets and pants that are waterproof and breathable, and have sufficient insulation. Also, consider the type of riding you will be doing - baggy clothing is ideal for freestyle, while form-fitting clothing is better for backcountry.

5. Helmet: A helmet is an essential piece of safety gear for any snowboarder. Look for helmets with proper ventilation, impact protection, and a comfortable fit. Also, consider the style of riding you will be doing - full-face helmets are ideal for backcountry, while half-shell helmets are better for park.

6. Gloves: Gloves are necessary to keep your hands warm and dry while riding. Choose gloves that are waterproof, breathable, and have enough insulation for the weather conditions you will be riding in. Also, consider the type of riding you will be doing - mittens offer better warmth for cold conditions, while gloves provide better dexterity for park riding.

7. Goggles: Goggles protect your eyes from the sun, wind, and snow while riding. Look for goggles with anti-fog technology, good ventilation, and a comfortable fit. The lens color should be appropriate for the weather conditions - lighter lenses for overcast days and darker lenses for sunny days.

Overall, selecting the right snowboarding gear requires you to consider your personal preferences, style of riding, and the terrain and weather conditions you will be riding in. By following these comprehensive tips, you can ensure that you have a comfortable, safe, and enjoyable snowboarding experience on the mountain. context:Snowboarding requires careful selection of equipment to ensure a safe and enjoyable experience on the mountain.
